citeAs: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov (2025). Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732.
creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov (PleIAs)
description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing approximately 2 trillion tokens (~1,998,647,168,282 tokens). The data is either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses, and covers a wide variety of languages (from major European languages to low-resource ones) as well as code data, spanning diverse genres, time periods, and domains across six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Code, Open Web, and Open Semantic.
inLanguage: en, fr, de, es, it, pt, pl, el, ru, la, nl, da, sv, cs, sr, ar, zh, ja, ko, lu, and many others (300+ languages including low-resource languages)
name: Common Corpus
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges several bias-related issues: (1) Historical texts in Open Culture (from the 18th–19th centuries or earlier) do not meet modern ethical standards regarding discussion of ethnic groups, women, and violence — a toxicity filtering pipeline was developed to mitigate this; (2) Open Science collection has less linguistic diversity, with nearly 85% of documents in English due to the specificity of open scientific publishing; (3) Coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow despite the dataset's multilingual nature; (4) The dataset does not contain instruction-tuning data, making it unsuitable for task-specific fine-tuning; (5) None of the curation methods can guarantee 100% accuracy, so some issues (e.g., residual OCR errors, toxicity) may remain.
rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from six collections: (1) Open Government — financial, legal, and administrative data from sources such as SEC filings, WTO documents, AMF documents, EU tenders, and GATT library; (2) Open Culture — cultural heritage datasets (monographs and periodicals) from institutions such as the French National Library (Gallica), Library of Congress, Internet Archive, Europeana, and national libraries across Europe; (3) Open Science — scientific papers and documents collected via OpenAlex API filtered by CC-By, Public Domain/CC0, and CC-By-SA licenses, plus arXiv and European-specific resources; (4) Open Code — code data from The Stack v1 and v2; (5) Open Web — Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons (CC-By audio transcripts), and StackExchange; (6) Open Semantic — Wikidata in natural language, covering 300 languages, in collaboration with Wikimedia Deutschland. Data was collected using APIs, bulk dumps (Collections As Data), and standard retrieval methods.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include: PDF documents (e.g., over 1.36 million original PDFs from AMF and WTO), digitized books and newspapers from cultural heritage institutions (with OCR output), scientific papers in PDF format from OpenAlex, source code files from GitHub (via The Stack v1 and v2 — 6.4TB and ~67.5TB respectively), Wikimedia HTML dumps, YouTube audio transcripts, StackExchange forum data, and Wikidata RDF dumps. Many sources were in raw XML (METS/ALTO), mediawiki syntax, or other domain-specific formats.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset covers documents spanning from the mid-20th century to 2024 for financial data (SEC reports from 1993–2024, WTO documents from 1995–2024), historical newspapers from as early as 1618 (Europeana Newspapers) and 1690 (US PD Newspapers) up to 1990, GATT documents from January 1, 1946 to September 6, 1996, and USPTO documents from 2019 to 2022. The dataset collection effort began in May 2023, with the first Common Corpus release in March 2024, and the current version released in February 2025.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus does not collect the full range of available open data (the "open data paradox"). Coverage for low-resource languages is shallow; plans exist to expand African language corpora (Swahili, Wolof, Bambara). The ~2 trillion tokens is suitable for pre-training models of limited size (as in the Pleias model family) but larger models require significantly more data. The dataset does not contain instruction-tuning data and is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. Curation methods (OCR correction, toxicity detection, PII removal) cannot guarantee 100% accuracy. Some historical texts may still contain content that does not meet modern ethical standards despite toxicity filtering.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For Open Culture and public domain data, documents containing harmful language were either removed or synthetically rewritten without the harmful language using the Celadon toxicity classifier. OCRonos was used to synthetically rewrite highly deteriorated OCR content. For Open Code, files were filtered by language/format extensions, license type, and digit content (removing files with 75%+ digits). Wikidata items were translated from RDF triples into natural language sequences (e.g., "Q41309 | P:27 | Q171150" → "Franz Liszt country of citizenship Kingdom of Hungary"), with all available translations provided as consecutive blocks separated by newlines.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing steps include: (1) Text segmentation using Segmentext, a model trained to handle broken/unstructured texts with digitization artifacts; (2) OCR quality detection using OCRoscope (based on cld2 language identification, measuring non-recognized 7-grams) and OCRerrcr (a DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters); (3) OCR correction using OCRonos (based on Llama 3 8B), correcting OCR errors, wrong word cuts/merges, and broken text structures; (4) PII removal using Microsoft Presidio with custom regular expression patterns, replacing PII with fictitious but realistic values; (5) Toxicity detection using Celadon (a DeBERTa-v3-small model ~140M parameters trained on 2M annotated samples), identifying toxic content along five dimensions; (6) For Open Code: removal of unwanted file types (SVG, CSV, JSON, etc.), license filtering, removal of files with 75%+ digits, and replacement of [\r]+\n sequences.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus is described as "an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset." HuggingFace ensures proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. Ongoing data collection is planned as part of the LLMs4EU project, with plans to expand corpora in African languages (Swahili, Wolof, Bambara) and continue collecting more data in European languages.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus aims to support the development of fully open and auditable LLMs that comply with AI legislation (including EU AI regulations) and data security regulations, without relying on copyrighted or proprietary content. It enables open science research on LLMs that was previously hindered by legal uncertainties. The dataset supports multilingual LLM development, including for lower-resource European languages, contributing to linguistic diversity in AI. It has been acknowledged as one of the main deliverables of the Paris AI Summit (February 2025) as the "largest open database to train Large Language Models." It has been used by industry leaders (Anthropic) and multiple European LLM projects, and serves as a shared research infrastructure for the open AI commons.
rai:dataUseCases: Primary use case is pre-training Large Language Models. Additional use cases include: training multilingual LLMs with diverse and creative writing styles; developing historical language models; training models for legal knowledge and document processing; training models for coding applications and improving natural language reasoning; developing vision-language models (VLMs) for document segmentation and processing; training models for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); creating multimodal datasets; developing speech foundation models; and serving as infrastructure for open science LLM research and development.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Several machine/ML tools were used in the pipeline: (1) Segmentext — a custom text segmentation model trained to handle digitization artifacts; (2) OCRoscope — a tool based on the cld2 language identification library for OCR quality detection; (3) OCRerrcr — a DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters for OCR error detection; (4) OCRonos — a model based on Llama 3 8B for OCR correction; (5) Celadon — a DeBERTa-v3-small model (~140M parameters) for multilingual toxicity classification; (6) Microsoft Presidio — for PII detection and removal; (7) fastText language identification model — for computing language distribution; (8) cld2 (pycld2) — for language identification in OCRoscope.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) was identified and removed from the dataset. PII includes phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses. Microsoft Presidio was used to detect PII, with custom regular expression patterns increasing phone number detection accuracy to 85%. PII was replaced with fictitious but realistic values rather than removed or tagged, to preserve text format while protecting individual identity.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: This is a pre-training corpus, not an annotated dataset; no per-item annotation count is described.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: No human annotators were used for labeling; the dataset is assembled from existing sources with automated processing.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No human annotation process with inter-annotator agreement metrics is described; data is assembled from existing licensed/public domain sources.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No annotation platform is used; the dataset is assembled from existing sources with automated curation tools.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: No human annotation protocol is described; data is assembled from existing licensed/public domain sources with automated processing.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling (e.g., cloud filtering, missing records). It mentions OCR quality issues but these are addressed through correction tools, not missing data imputation.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol for missing values is described in the paper.
null_reasons.license: No single dataset-level license is stated for Common Corpus itself. The paper describes licenses of the constituent source data (Public Domain, CC-By, MIT, CC-By-SA, Apache-2.0, etc.), and the HuggingFace listing also shows no license field.
